newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Bulgarian opera stars are enduring export.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bulgarian opera stars are enduring export.

text.p: Despite political upheaval and economic crisis, Bulgaria's opera singers have kept their place as one of the Balkan country's most enduring exports.

Singers like the late Boris Christoff and soprano Raina Kabaivanska are among more than a dozen who have won acclaim in opera houses like Milan's La Scala, London's Covent Garden and others around the world.
Bulgaria has seven opera houses of its own, and the art has always been so popular that even under communist rule singers were allowed to leave the country to perform abroad.
"Love of singing is in Bulgarians' genes," said opera critic Boyanka Arnaudova.

She said its roots lay in religious music and the development of folk traditions, especially under the 500 years of Ottoman rule until the 19th century. Choral singing has also developed rapidly since last century.
The best singers in a village sang when people gathered for celebrations or while harvesting, when their voices had been heard by everyone working in the field, she said.

"I think that part of the secret is in Bulgaria's beautiful nature and climate, the atmosphere and people's openness and fighting spirit," said soprano Anna Tomowa-Sintow, who is based mainly in Germany and performs all over the world.
"Singing has never been for me a way to build up a career, but joy and full devotion," said Tomowa-Sintow, who worked intensively for 16 years with conductor Herbert von Karajan.
OPERA POPULAR IN SPITE OF ECONOMIC HARDSHIP
Tickets for performances at Sofia's ornate opera house sell out despite the economic hardship affecting many people.

"I live with people's misery not only when I am in Bulgaria. But my heart is excited because in such a situation opera halls are full and the interest of the young people is getting greater and greater," Tomowa-Sintow said.
Christoff, the country's best known singer, never sang on a Bulgarian stage, though he recorded Orthodox church music in the gold-domed Aleksander Nevski cathedral in Sofia in 1976.

Early in his career he enjoyed the patronage of King Boris III. He left Bulgaria in 1942, two years before the communist takeover, and was prevented by the communist rulers from returning home for many years.
But Christoff remained a Bulgarian and was buried in Sofia after his death in 1993.
Nowadays he is often heard on Bulgarian radio as Boris in Modest Mussorgsky's opera "Boris Godunov" or in works by Borodin, Verdi, Puccini and Rossini.
Christoff's recording of the song "Mnogo Leto" (Long Life) is often played at celebrations and his resonant voice booms out on Bulgarian radio and television on New Year's Day.
Christoff lived most of his life in Italy, where Kabaivanska and bass Nikolay Gyaurov also live.
"I really feel a citizen of the world. I am adapting all the time to new cultures and languages, which is enormously interesting." said Gyaurov, who has spent 42 years on stage.
Kabaivanska, who has lived abroad for almost 40 years, said she had so many contracts until the end of the year that she will not have a free minute until December.
The beginnings of Bulgarian opera date from 1890 when three Bulgarians studying in Prague returned to Sofia to set up an opera troupe which lasted two seasons.
Another attempt to set up an opera house was made in 1908 and this time it won the support of the people.
"The opera is an enormous cultural inheritance which we have to preserve and hand over to the next generations," said Kabaivanska.
The idea of private sponsorship of art has not yet met much support among Bulgarian businessmen, although they helped the Sofia state opera stage an outdoor performance of Verdi's Aida this summer.
The former mausoleum of communist leader Georgi Dimitrov was transformed into an Egyptian pyramid for the occasion. The three performances, part of the Sofia Music Week Festival, were a sell-out.
